item.title: Ask the Right Question to Find the Right Answer
item.description:
Decision-Making

Ask the Right Question to Find the Right Answer

Before jumping to a solution, fully explore the underlying problem.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • It’s common to jump to solutions based on your own perception of a problem.
  • Instead, get the full context by talking to other people involved in the situation.
  • Restate the problem in a form that everyone agrees is accurate. Then solve it.

What do the following scenarios have in common?

  1. A manager notices an intern dressed inappropriately for the office. The next day, a memo is circulated to everyone in the office with a new dress code.
  2. A parent receives their teen’s report card, showing dropping grades. The parent grounds the teen for the weekend.
  3. A husband asks his spouse not to use their phone at the dinner table. The spouse says, “Don’t treat me like a child.”

The manager, parent, and husband in these scenarios are all trying to solve a problem that they perceive as being caused by another person.

We can think of the manager, parent, and husband in these scenarios as the “director,” and the intern, teen, and spouse as the “actor.” The actor does something the director perceives as a problem. The director imposes a solution.

But the director’s solution is likely to be ineffective.

The office workers will be annoyed and may be confused if the hastily written dress code prohibits clothes they normally wear. Meanwhile, the intern won’t read the memo.

The teen will stomp off to their room, spend the weekend scrolling social media, and their grades will continue to drop.

The spouse will resent the husband and will defiantly keep their phone out at all times.

What went wrong?

In each case, the director missed a key step in the problem-solving process: They did not communicate with the actor. As a result, they did not fully understand the problem. You can’t effectively solve a problem you don’t understand.

In addition, in each case, the director is imposing some action on the actor. The actor doesn’t necessarily understand why they have to do the action, or agree that it is useful. As a result, they will resist taking the action.

The bad report card is a symptom, not the problem

Let’s look more closely at scenario number two: the teen punished for a bad report card. In the parent’s mind, the “bad report card” is the problem. And perhaps the parent’s thought process is, “It’s my job to discipline my child. Grounding is a good way to do that.”

But the parent hasn’t talked to the teen to understand why their grades have dropped. Suppose the problem is that the teen has been increasingly depressed due to social isolation. In that case, the parent’s proposed solution is harmful.

The problem isn’t the report card. The report card is a symptom. The real problem is what underlies the symptom. That’s what needs to be solved.

Depending on what the problem is, the solution will be drastically different. If it’s social isolation, the parent might provide emotional support. If it’s an issue with handing in assignments, the parent could work with the teen and their teachers on executive function skills. If it’s a lack of sleep causing difficulty concentrating at school, the parent and teen might discuss strategies for restful nights.

How do you know if you’re solving the right problem?

While the scenarios above may seem straightforward, in real life, it can be tricky to identify when you’re trying to solve problems that you don’t fully understand. When you’re in the director role, how do you know when you don’t have the full picture? Use this four-step process.

Step 1: Who is harmed, and how?

Try to articulate the problem in terms of its harmful impact on a person or people.

Consider the bad report card. Who is this hurting, and how? The parent might decide that poor grades will hurt the teen’s future prospects.

At this stage, as the director, you might realize the only person impacted is you—and the solution lies entirely with you, not the actor. For example, if your coworker with chronic allergies drives you up the wall with constant sniffling, you might just need to deal with it, or wear earplugs, or move your desk. You can’t order your coworker to be healthier. Similarly, an exasperated parent might be tempted to discipline a rowdy toddler—but what needs to be fixed is the parent’s capacity for patience, not the toddler’s age-appropriate behavior.

Step 2: Talk to each other.

Discuss the problem with the actor.

How do they see the situation? Do they agree it’s a problem? If so, do they have any proposed solutions? In this stage, keep your ears open and listen far more than you talk. You need the actor’s help to learn as much as you can about the situation.

The teen might say, “I don’t care about my grades; I care about volunteering 20 hours a week at the hospital”—which comes as news to the parent.

The office dress code memo from the first scenario above shows how this step is often skipped in organizations. In this example, the manager avoids a potentially uncomfortable conversation by imposing an organization-wide solution. The manager could simply talk to the intern about workplace dress expectations—or the manager might realize, when asking “who is harmed, and how,” that this is a non-problem because nobody is harmed by the intern wearing a hoodie to work.

Step 3: Re-articulate the shared problem.

Restate the problem you identified in Step 1 in a way that both you and the actor can agree on. This is the actual problem that takes into account both the director’s observations and the actor’s context.

For example, “How can we balance school expectations with volunteer work?” Both the parent and the teen could agree that this is a problem deserving a solution.

Step 4: Come up with a solution.

Depending on the situation, you might do this alone or collaboratively with the actor. Either way, your solution will come closer to solving the shared problem, and since it takes the actor’s concerns into account, the actor is more likely to cooperate.

The problem-solving process in action

Let’s return to scenario number three, the phone-addicted spouse, to see the entire process in action.

Step 1: Who is harmed, and how?

The director thinks both he and the actor are harmed. They deserve each other’s attention at family mealtimes, and ignoring each other in favor of devices will weaken their marriage.

Step 2: Talk to each other.

Instead of beginning with judgment—“You’re always on your phone”—the director begins with a concern: “I want us to stay connected, so our marriage stays strong. I’ve noticed you’ve been keeping your phone on the table at dinner, and I feel like I can’t keep your attention.”

The actor responds, “I agreed to be available for emergency work calls in the evening. The extra pay is going toward our vacation. So I need my phone by my side.”

Step 3: Re-articulate the shared problem.

The director says, “I see. Could we find a way for you to be available for work but not be distracted by the phone when you’re not on a work call?”

Step 4: Come up with a solution.

They decide together that the phone will stay plugged in in the next room, but with the volume turned up so the actor will hear it ringing and can answer immediately.

Notice how different this solution is—and how different the problem is—than the husband-director’s original idea.

Next time you find yourself thinking that your problem would be solved if everyone would follow your directions, pause. Remind yourself that the problem, as you perceive it, is more likely to be a symptom than the real underlying problem. And then follow the steps above to get closer to an effective solution and a stronger relationship.

item.title: SNL’s ‘Sister’ Made America Laugh: Can It Change Who Cares?
item.description:
Caregiving

SNL’s ‘Sister’ Made America Laugh: Can It Change Who Cares?

How stories can change who provides care—and the support caregivers receive

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • SNL's "Sister" sketch shows how comedy can make caregiving responsibilities part of a national conversation.
  • Gender expectations shape who provides family care, leaving women with disproportionate responsibilities.
  • Research shows audiences want authentic portrayals of family relationships, work, and caregiving on screen.
  • Stories shift cultural norms and create opportunities for conversations about policies to help families.

This post is co-authored by Vicki Shabo, a senior fellow at New America, and Yalda T. Uhls, Ph.D.

Saturday Night Live’s November 14 sketch, “Sister”—a satirical, close-to-home ad for “sister” as America’s solution to a burgeoning caregiving tsunami—started a cultural conversation that has only grown. In a way that news stories, documentaries, and advocacy efforts couldn’t have dreamed of, this three-minute segment blew open a conversation America has long needed to have, not in the isolation of our own homes or whispered quietly in hours of exasperation and burnout, nor solely in the halls of legislatures, but in a true, fully open public square.

For both of us—a former movie executive-turned-developmental psychologist focused on using the reach and influence of pop culture to advance youth well-being and agency and a policy expert and advocate-turned-narrative change strategist with a focus on transforming television and film narratives about gender, work, family, and care—the ripple effects of the “Sister” sketch are a case study in how media helps people feel seen, valued, and understood—and provides hope for how media representation can spark cultural conversations that contribute to policy change.

The Caregiving Reality Behind the Comedy

“Sister” resonated because it said a quiet truth out loud: According to the National Alliance for Caregiving and AARP, there were 63 million caregivers to loved ones who are ill, disabled, or aging in the United States as of 2025, and six-in-10 were women—sisters, daughters, aunts, grandmothers, granddaughters, and female cousins. The experience of family caregiving is becoming more common: There were nearly 20 million more people in the U.S. providing care to loved ones in 2025 than there were 10 years before.

Some people choose to take on the care of a loved one, but more than half of caregivers said they had no choice. That’s, in part, because “choice” is too often a function of social expectations, gender dynamics that began in childhood, the economics of a gender-based wage gap that keeps women’s earnings lower than men’s and makes it more economically feasible for a woman to reduce work or leave a job (further exacerbating a wage and retirement savings gap).

Why a Three-Minute Comedy Sketch Went Viral

Why did a comedy sketch succeed in reaching so many people—traveling from private family and friend chats to social media to traditional print, radio, and television news outlets? Because stories can make complex social issues personal, relatable, and emotionally engaging. Rather than asking viewers to absorb another set of statistics about caregiving, “Sister” invited them to recognize a familiar family dynamic and laugh at its absurdity. Humor made an uncomfortable truth easier to confront, while the sketch’s specificity made it widely recognizable. And in today’s fragmented media landscape, a short, shareable piece of entertainment can move rapidly across generations, platforms, and communities, reaching people who might never read a policy report or seek out information about caregiving.

Caregiving is having a moment. The stories that “Sister” sparked, and facts about caregiving in America, have inspired public dialogue ranging from personal testimonials to a long-overdue conversation about the country’s lack of support for caregivers, including the high costs of care that the general public underestimates and the lack of policies to support families with care needs.

What Audiences Want to See on Screen

From a media research perspective, the power of this sketch is also no surprise. Media consumers in the United States are hungry to see stories about work, family, and care on screen. Research conducted for New America’s Re-Scripting Gender, Work, Family, and Care project in 2025 found that 92 percent of viewers aged 18 to 59 said that seeing relatable depictions of work and family woven into characters’ lives in television and film is important to them; yet as of just a few years ago, fewer than 11 percent of U.S. television shows depict caregiving.

U.S. television and film viewers—like Americans overall—are also eager for solutions: 70 percent of all viewers said in the New America research said that America should do more to support the needs, challenges, and financial costs of family members caring for older adults, and 82 percent said they believe families and communities and the economy would be more stable if the United States had national policies like paid family and medical leave and affordable elder care that make it easier for Americans to work and care for their loved ones.

Young Audiences Are Ready for More Authentic Stories

Young audiences are especially important to this conversation. At the Center for Scholars & Storytellers at UCLA (CSS), our annual Teens and Screens research has consistently found that young people want more authentic, relatable stories about their lives and relationships. They are increasingly interested in stories grounded in family, friendship, and community rather than sensationalized drama. These findings challenge the assumption that younger viewers are interested only in escapism. They also suggest an opportunity for storytellers to explore how young people experience family responsibilities, intergenerational relationships, and care—not just as background details, but as meaningful parts of their lives. New America’s research shows the same is true for adults.

We also know that changing what appears on screen doesn’t have to be left to chance. Both of our organizations work directly with writers, producers, and entertainment executives to translate research into practical storytelling guidance. At CSS, our work on the portrayal of boys and masculinity, for example, has helped creators think more deeply about vulnerability, friendship, and emotional expression. At New America, we’re doing the same for representation of how people manage the demands of work and family life with caregiving. Soon-to-be-released qualitative research reaffirms what survey data has already demonstrated: that audiences are tired of exhausted daughters in television scripts and eager to see men competently sharing, or leading on, family care. We’ve both heard directly from television creators about how these insights have influenced their thinking and storytelling choices.

How Hollywood Can Help Rewrite the Story of Care

We know that media that sparks viewers’ imagination, engagement, and conversation often encourages producers, writers, and executives to replicate resonant and popular cultural content. And we know that more media depictions can lead to widespread culture and policy change.

What if “Sister” was just the beginning of a media representation revolution that brings family conversations about caregiving into the light? What if every show or film considered a character’s caregiving responsibilities, family relationships, finances, and job responsibilities as an element of a backstory or the on-screen story?

At a time when millions of Americans are navigating the challenges of care, these stories could do more than entertain. They could help people feel seen, challenge assumptions about gender and family, and expand our collective imagination about what is possible.

“Sister” made America laugh at an uncomfortable truth. Now Hollywood has an opportunity to help us imagine something different.

item.title: You Don’t Need “Pure” Motives to Be a Good Person
item.description:
Altruism

You Don’t Need “Pure” Motives to Be a Good Person

Being good doesn't mean sacrificing yourself, but caring about others as well.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Having mixed motives doesn't have to diminish the goodness of an action or make our concerns insincere.
  • Self-interest becomes selfishness when we disregard other people's legitimate interests in pursuing our own.
  • When we care about others, their well-being can become part of our own interests.

In one of my business ethics classes, a student questioned how to think about his own volunteering. He said that he enjoyed the work and cared about the people he worked with, but he also knew that it would look good on his resume. He wondered whether having mixed motives took something away from volunteering. When I looked around the room, I saw most, if not all, heads nodding, sharing his doubts.

We sometimes assume that for an action to be truly moral, it must be altruistic. Neera Kapur Badhwar has shown the prominence of this idea in modern moral philosophy: that only acts motivated to help others for their own sake count as moral. This idea assumes that being self-interested means focusing on ourselves to the exclusion of others. That is why my students worry that wanting to volunteer but also seeing its benefit tarnishes the goodness of volunteering.

This form of thinking doesn’t distinguish between benefiting from an action, being motivated by that benefit, and acting exclusively for that benefit. It misunderstands human motivation and what it means to be selfish.

We Can Have More Than One Reason for Acting

If you’ve ever watched television shows like Succession, you can appreciate how easy it is to become cynical about people’s motivations. Every action is strategic, every act of generosity comes with conditions, and every relationship is ultimately a calculation for the sake of personal benefit. Yet, while people certainly can rationalize selfish behavior or disguise selfish motives with moral justifications, for most of us, personal benefit isn’t the only thing motivating us. In fact, Grant and Berry have shown that prosocial and self-oriented motives need not be at odds. When people care about helping others, they are more likely to take other people’s perspectives and channel their intrinsic motivation into ideas that are both novel and useful.

So, while a desire to boost one’s resume may motivate people to do something, it doesn’t mean that the choice of what to do is insincere. My student volunteered both because he wanted to help others and because doing so might benefit him. Moreover, the relative importance of each motive may change depending on the day, the circumstances of the situation, or the task you are performing.

Recognizing that we have multiple motives for doing something is not an admission of moral weakness. It is an appreciation for the complexity of human motivation.

Self-Interest Is Different From Selfishness

Self-interest means being concerned about your own well-being and pursuing things that you care about. Selfishness means giving your own interests disproportionate priority when the legitimate interests of others should also matter. The difference between self-interest and selfishness is in how we consider other people’s legitimate interests when deciding what to do.

For example, wanting to advance your career is self-interested, yet it only becomes selfish when you take advantage of or disregard others to do so. When my student decided to volunteer, he was self-interested, yet, at the same time, he considered the needs of others in choosing to do so. He did not use others merely as a means for his own career advancement.

When Other People’s Interests Become Our Own

In his book The Reasons of Love, philosopher Harry Frankfurt gives an example of when self-interest and selflessness align rather than conflict. He writes that when you genuinely love someone, you do not care about their well-being simply because it makes you feel good. You care about their well-being for their sake. Yet, because you love them, their well-being has also become something in which you are personally invested, and caring about them does in fact make you feel good. Arthur Aron and colleagues have shown that when people become close, they incorporate aspects of the other person into their own self-concept. When this happens, caring for oneself and caring for another person need not be opposing motivations.

As a parent, I derive tremendous joy from seeing my children happy. Yet I do not want my children to be happy simply so that I can experience that joy. I want them to be happy because I love them. The satisfaction I derive from caring for them is not what motivates me, but it is a benefit that I enjoy.

When we love someone, their well-being becomes something we care about for its own sake, even when pursuing it requires us to set aside something else we want. When we choose a loved one’s well-being over other wants we have, we do not need to see this as acting self-sacrificially. We can recognize that we are pursuing something that we want over other things.

As our commitments to others and our communities grow, acting for the sake of others may not simply be a means for self-interested reciprocity, but rather can be grounded in a desire for relationship. Rather than making our actions less ethical, it deepens the moral community in which we live.

Asking Better Questions About Our Motivations

Rather than requiring your motivations to be completely altruistic, to assess the goodness of your actions, ask yourself the following questions:

  • In pursuing what I want, am I only considering my own interests or am I thinking about others as well?
  • Am I motivated solely by personal benefit, or is the benefit I get from this only one motivation among others?
  • How can I pursue my own interests in ways that do not harm or disregard others?

These questions can help us recognize when we might be acting selfishly rather than with self-interest and how we can do good while pursuing the things we care about.

Being a good person does not require eliminating self-interest or denying yourself the satisfaction or benefit you get from doing good things. Rather, it means developing the capacity to care about others and to consider their interests alongside your own. When we do this, we can recognize that it can—and should—feel good to do good things.
